Composing immune modules with AINet

Nick Borcherding

Washington University in St. Louis, School of Medicine, St. Louis, MO, USA
ncborch@gmail.com

2026-10-16

Source: vignettes/immune-modules.Rmd
immune-modules.Rmd
library(bHIVE)
## Warning: replacing previous import 'S4Arrays::makeNindexFromArrayViewport' by
## 'DelayedArray::makeNindexFromArrayViewport' when loading 'SummarizedExperiment'

Introduction

The bHIVE package has two interfaces. The functional bHIVE() runs a whole analysis in one call, and the introductory vignette, vignette("bHIVE", package = "bHIVE"), uses it on mass cytometry data. The R6 class AINet exposes the same engine as a model object. This vignette covers AINet and the nine immune modules it accepts, each of which changes one stage of the algorithm. We use the small iris data so each example runs in a second.

Each module is an independent R6 class that encapsulates a single immunological mechanism. You create modules separately and pass them to AINet$new(), allowing you to mix and match any combination.

model <- AINet$new(
  nAntibodies = 20,
  shm            = SHMEngine$new(method = "adaptive"),
  idiotypic      = IdiotypicNetwork$new(),
  germinalCenter = GerminalCenter$new(),
  microenvironment = Microenvironment$new(),
  init           = VDJLibrary$new(method = "pca"),
  activation     = ActivationGate$new(),
  memory         = MemoryPool$new()
)

Somatic Hypermutation Engine

The SHMEngine controls how antibodies mutate after cloning. Five strategies are available, each grounded in a different aspect of SHM biology:

Method Biological Analogy When to Use
"uniform" Random point mutations Baseline; simple and robust
"airs" Affinity-proportional mutation (AIRS) When high-affinity antibodies should explore less
"hotspot" AID targets WRCY motifs When some features matter more than others
"energy" E_SHM ~ N_Mut^2 budget constraint When you want bounded total perturbation
"adaptive" Per-feature Adam-like moment tracking Best for complex landscapes; most novel

The adaptive method is the most distinctive in which somatic hypermutation and the Adam optimizer function the same. Each feature dimension maintains running mean and variance of past gradients.

data(iris)
X <- as.matrix(iris[, 1:4])
y <- iris$Species

set.seed(3)
methods <- c("uniform", "airs", "adaptive")
results <- lapply(methods, function(m) {
  shm <- SHMEngine$new(method = m)
  model <- AINet$new(nAntibodies = 15, 
                     maxIter = 15, 
                     shm = shm,
                     verbose = FALSE)
  model$fit(X, y, task = "classification")
  data.frame(
    method   = m,
    accuracy = mean(model$result$assignments == as.character(y)),
    n_ab     = nrow(model$repertoire$as_matrix())
  )
})
do.call(rbind, results)
##     method  accuracy n_ab
## 1  uniform 0.8000000   12
## 2     airs 0.7266667   10
## 3 adaptive 0.9466667   15

Idiotypic Network Regulation

In classical AIS, similar antibodies are suppressed via a simple distance threshold (epsilon). The IdiotypicNetwork module replaces this with network dynamics inspired by Varela and Coutinho’s (1991) second-generation immune network theory.

The key idea is a bell-shaped activation function. Too little stimulation from other antibodies leads to death, moderate stimulation to activation, and excessive stimulation to suppression.

The module is experimental. It applies the activation to each pair of antibodies, so it works as intended on a small, tight repertoire. The example below builds one: four antibodies at pairwise affinity 0.25, in the middle of the default activation window, and one far from the rest.

a <- sqrt(log(4) / 2)
A <- rbind(cbind(diag(4) * a, 0), c(0, 0, 0, 0, 10))
rep <- ImmuneRepertoire$new(A)
idi <- IdiotypicNetwork$new(theta_low = 0.01, theta_high = 0.5)
idi$regulate(rep, "gaussian", list(alpha = 1))
idi
## <IdiotypicNetwork>
##   Activation window: [0.010, 0.500]
##   Dynamics: 20 steps (dt=0.100)
##   Source: 0.500  Decay: 0.100  Survival: 0.500
##   Last run: 4/5 antibodies survived
round(as.vector(idi$get_population()), 2)
## [1] 1.73 1.73 1.73 1.73 0.12

The four antibodies that stimulate each other survive. The isolated one is under-stimulated and dies.

On a full repertoire most pairs of antibodies are far apart. Their affinity is near zero, below theta_low, so each pair counts as suppression and the dynamics remove every antibody. AINet then keeps the top 10% by population and reports it:

set.seed(1)
model_idi <- AINet$new(nAntibodies = 25, maxIter = 15,
                       idiotypic = IdiotypicNetwork$new(),
                       verbose = FALSE)
model_idi$fit(X, task = "clustering")
## IdiotypicNetwork removed every antibody in 1 of 15 iterations; the top 10% by population were kept each time. See ?IdiotypicNetwork for when the module applies.
model_idi$repertoire$size()
## [1] 2

Check that antibodies survive on your data before relying on this module. A field-based form, in which the activation acts on the total stimulation each antibody receives, is planned.

Germinal Center Selection

The GerminalCenter module models the competition for T follicular helper (Tfh) cell help that occurs in real germinal centers. Only antibodies that receive Tfh help survive – this implements quality-based selection pressure.

The quality metric is task-aware:

  • Classification: proportion of correctly matched labels
  • Clustering: local density (sum of affinities to assigned data points)
gc <- GerminalCenter$new(
  nTfh = 20,                 # number of Tfh selectors
  selectionPressure = 0.2,   # 0 = no selection, 1 = very strict
  rounds = 1
)

set.seed(4)
model_gc <- AINet$new(
  nAntibodies = 30, 
  maxIter = 15,
  germinalCenter = gc,
  verbose = FALSE
)
model_gc$fit(X, y, task = "classification")
c(antibodies = model_gc$repertoire$size(),
  accuracy = mean(model_gc$predict(X) == y))
## antibodies   accuracy 
## 17.0000000  0.8533333

Selection pressure trades repertoire size for quality. Strong pressure trims the repertoire hard and, on a small dataset like iris, can cost accuracy. Tune it against a model without the module.

Microenvironment

The Microenvironment module classifies the local context around each antibody into three zones and adapts mutation rates accordingly:

  • Stable (high local density): reduce mutation rate to preserve good antibodies
  • Explore (low local density): increase mutation rate to search sparse regions
  • Boundary (intermediate): moderate mutation, potential trigger for class switching
me <- Microenvironment$new(
  high_density_threshold = 0.75,
  low_density_threshold = 0.25,
  stabilization_factor = 0.3,   # reduce mutation to 30% in stable zones
  exploration_factor = 2.0      # double mutation in exploration zones
)

rep <- ImmuneRepertoire$new(X[sample(150, 15), ])
env <- me$assess(rep, X)
table(env$zones)
## 
## boundary  explore   stable 
##        7        4        4

V(D)J Gene Library Initialization

Instead of random sampling, VDJLibrary generates antibodies by combinatorial assembly of gene segments, mimicking V(D)J recombination. The feature space is split into three segments (V, D, J), each discretized into alleles, and new antibodies are built by combining one allele from each segment.

vdj <- VDJLibrary$new(nV = 5, 
                      nD = 3, 
                      nJ = 3, 
                      method = "pca")
A <- vdj$generate(20, X)
dim(A)  # 20 antibodies x 4 features
## [1] 20  4
print(vdj)
## <VDJLibrary> method='pca' V=5 D=3 J=3
##   Combinatorial space: 45 antibodies

Three decomposition methods are available:

  • "pca": PCA components define gene segments (best for correlated features)
  • "cluster": k-means within dimension groups creates alleles
  • "random_partition": random feature grouping (simplest)

Two-Signal Activation Gate

In real immunity, B cells require two signals to activate: antigen recognition (Signal 1) and costimulatory context (Signal 2). The ActivationGate module prevents spurious cloning on isolated outliers.

Signal 2 options:

  • "density": local data density around the antibody
  • "danger": user-provided danger score per data point
  • "entropy": local label entropy (classification only)
gate <- ActivationGate$new(
  signal2_type = "density",
  threshold1 = 0.1,    # minimum affinity (Signal 1)
  threshold2 = 0.3     # density percentile (Signal 2)
)

A <- X[sample(150, 10), ]
rep <- ImmuneRepertoire$new(A)
aff <- rep$affinity_matrix(X, "gaussian")
activated <- gate$evaluate(aff, X, A)
c(activated = sum(activated), total = length(activated))
## activated     total 
##       413      1500

Memory Pool

The MemoryPool archives high-performing antibodies and recalls them when relevant to current data. This is useful for streaming or non-stationary data where distribution shifts may occur.

mp <- MemoryPool$new(
  archive_threshold = 0.01,  # minimum average affinity to archive
  max_memory = 50,
  recall_threshold = 0.01
)

rep <- ImmuneRepertoire$new(X[sample(150, 10), ])
mp$archive(rep, X)
## [1] 10
mp
## <MemoryPool> 10 cells (max 50)
##   Archive threshold: 0.010
##   Recall threshold:  0.010
# Recall memories relevant to a subset
recalled <- mp$recall(X[1:30, ])
nrow(recalled)
## [1] 4

Class Switcher

The ClassSwitcher module changes the effective kernel width of antibodies based on their microenvironment zone, analogous to real B cell isotype switching:

Isotype Kernel Width Matching Style
IgM alpha = 0.1 Broad (exploration)
IgG alpha = 5.0 Specific (discrimination)
IgA alpha = 1.0 Intermediate (boundary patrol) 
cs <- ClassSwitcher$new(alpha_IgM = 0.1, alpha_IgG = 5.0, alpha_IgA = 1.0)

rep <- ImmuneRepertoire$new(X[sample(150, 10), ])
zones <- sample(c("stable", "explore", "boundary"), 10, replace = TRUE)
alphas <- cs$switch_isotypes(rep, zones)
data.frame(zone = zones, isotype = rep$metadata$isotype, alpha = alphas)
##        zone isotype alpha
## 1   explore     IgM   0.1
## 2    stable     IgG   5.0
## 3  boundary     IgA   1.0
## 4    stable     IgG   5.0
## 5    stable     IgG   5.0
## 6  boundary     IgA   1.0
## 7    stable     IgG   5.0
## 8  boundary     IgA   1.0
## 9    stable     IgG   5.0
## 10  explore     IgM   0.1

Convergent Selection

The ConvergentSelector identifies “public antibodies” – antibodies that appear across multiple independent bHIVE runs. This implements the immunological concept of public clonotypes as a biologically-motivated ensemble method.

# Run 3 independent bHIVE analyses
set.seed(42)
results <- lapply(1:3, function(i) {
  m <- AINet$new(nAntibodies = 15, maxIter = 10, verbose = FALSE)
  m$fit(X, task = "clustering")
  m$result
})

conv <- ConvergentSelector$new(tolerance = 1.0, min_appearances = 2)
public <- conv$from_results(results)
nrow(public)
## [1] 12

Putting It All Together

Here is a full example combining multiple modules for a classification task:

set.seed(2)
model <- AINet$new(
  nAntibodies = 25,
  maxIter = 20,
  k = 3,
  beta = 5,
  shm = SHMEngine$new(method = "adaptive", base_rate = 0.1),
  germinalCenter = GerminalCenter$new(nTfh = 8, selectionPressure = 0.4),
  microenvironment = Microenvironment$new(),
  classSwitcher = ClassSwitcher$new(),
  verbose = FALSE
)

model$fit(X, y, task = "classification")
model
## <AINet>
##   Repertoire: 9 antibodies x 4 features
##   Task: classification
##   Iterations: 20
mean(model$predict(X) == y)
## [1] 0.82

Not every module combination improves every dataset. Compare a combination against the plain AINet before keeping it, on held-out data or with cross-validation. caret::train(method = bHIVEmodel) passes extra arguments, modules included, on to bHIVE().
